holding_summary: After a Canara Bank employee died intestate, his widow and his mother both claimed posthumous terminal benefits of about Rs. 62.90 lakh, with the mother relying on her status as the nominee recorded in the bank's records. Justice Biraja Prasanna Satapathy held that nomination in a bank account or insurance policy does not amount to ownership — a nominee merely holds the proceeds as a trustee for the legal heirs — and that under Hindu succession law the property of a male Hindu dying intestate devolves first upon his Class I heirs, including his widow, ahead of any nominee's claim.
why_it_matters: A bank, insurer or company nominee recorded on an account or policy is not thereby made the legal owner of the proceeds — the deceased's actual legal heirs under succession law retain the superior claim, so families should not assume a nomination alone settles who is entitled to a deceased relative's funds.

case_name: Sri Venkataiah v. State of Karnataka & Ors.
holding_summary: An 84-year-old illiterate senior citizen sought annulment of a gift deed executed in favour of his daughters, contending it was drafted at his daughters' instance with him merely affixing a thumb impression without understanding its contents, and that the assurance to maintain him — though the very basis of the transfer — had been deliberately omitted from the document. The Karnataka High Court held that a legal representative of the original donee cannot independently resist annulment of a gift deed under Section 23 of the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 by raising derivative defences that were unavailable to the donee, once the statutory conditions for revocation are otherwise met.
why_it_matters: A senior citizen seeking to reclaim property transferred in exchange for an implied or express promise of maintenance can have that gift deed annulled even where the promise was never written into the document, and the donee's own legal heirs cannot resist that annulment by raising defences the original donee themselves could not have raised.

case_name: Ashok Shankar v. Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax
court: Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Delhi Bench
holding_summary: The taxpayer had failed to disclose a foreign bank account and his shareholding in a UAE company in his income tax return. The Delhi Bench of the ITAT upheld the income tax demand and penalty levied under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015, holding that a foreign bank account cannot be left undisclosed merely because it has few transactions, and that non-disclosure of a foreign asset — together with a failure to explain its source — attracts action under the Act even where some related income was otherwise reported.
why_it_matters: NRIs and returning residents with foreign bank accounts or overseas shareholdings should treat full Schedule FA disclosure in their Indian income tax return as non-negotiable — a dormant account with minimal activity, or a shareholding whose related income was reported elsewhere, does not excuse leaving the underlying asset itself undisclosed.

case_name: Gur Kaur (Minor) & Ors. v. Union of India & Anr.
holding_summary: Adoptive parents who had completed a registered adoption of a minor child under the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, including verification by the District Magistrate, sought CARA's No Objection Certificate to relocate the child to Canada, but CARA issued only a support letter rather than the NOC needed for the destination country's immigration process. Justice Sachin Datta held that CARA is statutorily obligated under the Adoption Regulations to facilitate compliance with the Hague Convention on Intercountry Adoption for such relocations, and cannot leave adoptive parents without effective recourse merely because the underlying adoption was completed under HAMA rather than the Juvenile Justice Act.
why_it_matters: Families who have adopted a child under Hindu personal law and later need to relocate abroad now have High Court authority that CARA cannot fob them off with an informal support letter — it must actively process Hague Convention documentation needed for the destination country to recognise the adoption and grant the child entry.

case_name: In re: Adoption of a Minor by an NRI Relative (US-based aunt) v. Union of India (CARA)
holding_summary: A 13-year-old girl, adopted under a registered adoption deed by her maternal aunt and uncle (resident in the United States) under the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 following her mother's death in July 2024, challenged a CARA office memorandum of 9 February 2026 that blocked processing of the inter-country relative adoption. At a hearing on 22 June 2026, a Bench of Justices B.V. Nagarathna and Joymalya Bagchi questioned CARA's opposition to adoption by close family members and expressed dissatisfaction with the administrative hurdles facing relatives seeking to care for the child, listing the matter for further hearing; the case remains pending and no final order has issued as of the date of this note.
why_it_matters: NRI relatives seeking to formalise or relocate a child already adopted by them under personal law should watch this case closely — the Supreme Court's early remarks suggest it may curb CARA's practice of treating a relative adoption already completed under HAMA as ineligible for inter-country adoption clearance, though the point is not yet finally decided.

holding_summary: A Karta of a Hindu joint family had unilaterally executed a settlement/gift deed transferring an entire item of ancestral property to one coparcener, without the consent of the other coparcerners, including minors. Dr. Justice A.D. Maria Clete held that a Karta has no absolute authority to make such a unilateral gift of the whole or a substantial portion of joint family property, describing it as a 'virtual partition by gift' — a concept unknown to Hindu law and wholly outside a Karta's competence — and declared the settlement deed void ab initio.
why_it_matters: A Karta cannot use a gift or settlement deed to informally favour one coparcener with the family's joint property over the others — any such unilateral transfer of a substantial portion of joint family property is void from the outset and can be challenged by the excluded coparceners regardless of how long it has stood.

case_name: Dorairaj v. Doraisamy (Dead) Thr. LRs & Ors.
holding_summary: In a long-running partition dispute over 79 items of agricultural property in Perambalur Taluk, Tiruchirappalli District, originating from a 1987 suit, a Bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and Satish Chandra Sharma held that once the existence of an ancestral, income-yielding nucleus of property is established, acquisitions subsequently made by the family's Karta during the subsistence of the joint Hindu family are ordinarily presumed to be joint family property. The burden then shifts to the person claiming the acquisition was instead the Karta's self-acquired, individual property to discharge that burden with cogent evidence, rather than the other coparceners having to prove the acquisition was made with joint family funds.
why_it_matters: A coparcener seeking a share of property acquired by the family's Karta during the joint family's existence does not need to trace the exact funds used for that specific acquisition — once an income-yielding ancestral nucleus is shown to have existed, the burden shifts to the Karta (or whoever claims the property as self-acquired) to prove it with solid evidence, not mere assertion.

case_name: Dr. Govindaraja Venkatesh Iyengar v. A.R. Sampathkumar (Deceased) Thr. LRs & Ors.
citation: Testamentary Suit No. 42 of 2012 in Testamentary Petition No. 64 of 2011
holding_summary: The executor named in a Will dated 22 December 1998 of Rajalakshmi Gopal Ayengar sought probate nearly two decades later, facing objections alleging fraud, forgery and invalid execution, alongside the nine-year delay between the testator's death and the probate petition being pursued to hearing. Justice N.J. Jamadar granted probate, holding the case was supported by unusually strong direct evidence — both attesting witnesses confirmed the testator signed the Will in their presence — and that the objectors had failed to substantiate the forgery and suspicious-circumstances allegations, while the delay itself, though noted, did not defeat an otherwise well-proved Will.
why_it_matters: Neither a long delay in seeking probate nor a bare allegation of forgery will defeat an otherwise properly executed and well-evidenced Will — objectors challenging a Will need to actually substantiate forgery or suspicious circumstances with real evidence, not merely raise the allegation and rely on the passage of time.

case_name: M. Gagan Bothra v. Senthil Kumar & Anr.
court: National Company Law Tribunal, Chennai (Division Bench-I)
holding_summary: After a resolution plan for corporate debtor PRC International Hotels Private Limited left Rs. 14.92 crore of a personal guarantee outstanding, the guarantor argued he was now a permanent resident of New Jersey, USA and held no assets in India. Judicial Member Sanjiv Jain and Technical Member Venkataraman Subramaniam admitted the Section 95 IBC petition against him regardless, holding that the Code's provisions on personal guarantor insolvency do not restrict their applicability based on the guarantor's nationality, citizenship or place of residence, and appointed a Resolution Professional.
why_it_matters: An Indian personal guarantee does not become unenforceable simply because the guarantor later relocates abroad, changes citizenship, or holds no assets in India at the time of the claim — lenders can pursue Section 95 insolvency proceedings against an overseas guarantor in the same way as a resident one, and prospective guarantors abroad should treat an Indian personal guarantee as following them regardless of where they later live.

case_name: Principal Commissioner of Income Tax v. Samsung India Electronics Pvt. Ltd.
holding_summary: The Revenue filed Special Leave Petitions against a Delhi High Court judgment that had dismissed the Income Tax Department's appeal challenging transfer pricing adjustments on Samsung India's royalty payments to Samsung Korea. The Supreme Court dismissed the Revenue's SLPs, citing unexplained delays of 609 and 457 days in filing, while keeping the underlying questions of law open for a future case.
why_it_matters: The Revenue's own delay in approaching the Supreme Court let a taxpayer-favourable Delhi High Court ruling on royalty-payment transfer pricing stand undisturbed — a reminder that procedural delay by the tax department can itself decide the outcome of an appeal, even where the substantive questions remain formally open.

case_name: Impresario Entertainment and Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. v. The Shake Social (trading as Social Circle)
holding_summary: Building on its January 2026 declaration of 'SOCIAL' as a well-known trademark in a related suit, Justice Vikas Mahajan granted an interim injunction restraining a Dehradun restaurant trading as 'Social Circle' from using a mark deceptively similar to Impresario's 'SOCIAL' brand for restaurant and bar services.
why_it_matters: Once a mark is judicially recognised as well-known, the owner can secure fast interim relief against confusingly similar names used by unrelated restaurants and outlets in other cities, without having to re-litigate the mark's reputation each time.

holding_summary: A Bench of Justice N. Seshasayee and Jatindranath Swain upheld the Committee of Creditors' decision to replace a resolution professional, holding that such a replacement falls within the CoC's commercial wisdom, provided the statutory route is followed, and that the Tribunal cannot interfere with it. The Bench cautioned that an RP must still function independently and not at the whims of a dominant creditor, but left the replaced RP's claim for professional fees and CIRP expenses open for adjudication by the NCLT.
why_it_matters: Resolution professionals should be aware that a CoC's decision to replace them, once the statutory procedure is followed, will attract the same judicial deference as other commercial decisions of the CoC — an RP's recourse for unpaid fees lies in a separate claim before the NCLT, not in resisting the replacement itself.

case_name: Vasavi Realtors LLP v. Telangana Real Estate Regulatory Authority & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Chairperson Justice A. Santhosh Reddy, Judicial Member P. Pradeep Kumar Reddy and Administrative Member Vemula Sreekar dismissed 31 appeals by Vasavi Realtors against Telangana RERA orders in its 'Vasavi Lake City-West' project at Hafeezpet, holding that extension of a project's RERA registration does not automatically extend the possession date already agreed with homebuyers, and that a promoter cannot unilaterally alter that contractual date. The developer was held liable for delayed possession beyond 28 February 2025 and directed to pay 10.70% annual interest on amounts paid by homebuyers until possession.
why_it_matters: Developers cannot rely on a registration extension granted by RERA to excuse delay against the possession date actually promised to homebuyers in their agreements for sale — the two timelines are legally independent, and delay-interest liability runs from the agreed date regardless of any registration extension.

holding_summary: A customer deposited two cheques worth over Rs. 1.06 crore with Canara Bank on 29 May 2018, but the bank failed to present them for clearance within their validity period, so they were returned as stale. A Bench of Justices B.V. Nagarathna and Ujjal Bhuyan upheld the NCDRC's finding that this delay amounted to deficiency in service under the Consumer Protection Act, while reducing the compensation awarded from 10% to 6% of the cheque amount with interest, holding banks to a duty of timely presentation absent any reasonable explanation for delay.
why_it_matters: Banks that sit on deposited cheques past their validity period without a genuine justification face consumer-forum liability for the resulting loss — account holders whose cheques lapse into staleness due to a bank's own delay have a clear Supreme Court precedent to rely on, though the compensation actually awarded may be moderated rather than matched fully to the cheque value.

case_name: N. Balakrishnan v. Tamil Nadu Real Estate Regulatory Authority & Ors.
holding_summary: A Thiruneermalai resident who claimed ownership of land in Tambaram challenged TNRERA's registration of a rival developer's project over the same land. Justice D. Bharatha Chakravarthy held that TNRERA cannot adjudicate a disputed question of title while examining a project registration application, and that a party disputing ownership of land underlying a registered project must approach the competent civil court instead.
why_it_matters: A landowner who believes a builder has registered a RERA project over land they actually own cannot expect RERA itself to resolve that ownership dispute — registration proceeds on the developer's declared title, and a genuine title contest has to be litigated separately in a civil suit, which can leave the project registered and moving forward while the title question is still pending.

case_name: M/s Goodluck India Limited & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.
holding_summary: Rule 96(10) of the CGST Rules, 2017, which had restricted exporters from claiming IGST refunds on exports where inputs were procured using specified concessional-duty benefits, was omitted with effect from 8 October 2024 by Notification No. 20/2024-Central Tax without any saving clause. A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran dismissed the Revenue's appeals and held that, in the absence of a saving clause, the omission of Rule 96(10) applies to every refund proceeding that was still pending on the date of omission, effectively ending such proceedings in the exporters' favour.
why_it_matters: Exporters with IGST refund claims that were held up or denied under the now-omitted Rule 96(10) should revisit those pending proceedings — the Supreme Court's ruling that the omission applies retrospectively to pending matters (absent a saving clause) gives them a clear basis to press for the refund rather than accept a denial issued under the repealed restriction.

case_name: Nikhil Rai & Anr. v. VCare Technologies Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
holding_summary: The NCLT had dismissed, on 9 July 2026, a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement in VCare Technologies Pvt. Ltd. after the respondents defended the impugned restructuring as commercially necessary. A Bench of Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma, Arun Baroka and Indevar Pandey set aside that dismissal and remanded the matter, holding that a respondent's detailed commercial justification for a restructuring does not by itself dispense with the adjudicating authority's duty to examine an oppression and mismanagement petition on the entire material on record.
why_it_matters: A company facing an oppression and mismanagement petition cannot expect a restructuring to be waved through merely by offering a plausible commercial rationale for it — the NCLT must still weigh the minority shareholder's actual evidence and grievance against that rationale, rather than treating a commercial explanation as an automatic defence.

case_name: Lachchappa and Others v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, UKP, Bagalkot and Others
holding_summary: Farmers whose agricultural land in Mudhol Village, Bagalkot District, Karnataka was acquired under a 1999 notification for a resettlement project sought the same enhanced compensation rate the reference court had already awarded to other landowners covered by the identical notification, despite a long delay in pursuing their own claim. A Bench of Justices S.V.N. Bhatti and N.V. Anjaria invoked Article 142 to hold that abnormal delay in claiming compensation is not, by itself, a bar to compensation parity among landowners whose land was acquired under the very same acquisition notification, and enhanced the appellants' compensation to Rs. 6,50,000 per acre with statutory benefits.
why_it_matters: Farmers and other landowners whose agricultural land was acquired years ago under a notification that has since yielded a higher compensation rate for their neighbours should not assume a long delay in raising their own claim is fatal — the Supreme Court's parity principle gives them a real basis to seek the same enhanced rate, even after considerable delay, where the acquisition notification is common.
